P3L4: Speed and Collision Outcomes

Student Science Notebook

Part 1: Speed and Collisions

Question: How will the speed of a vehicle at the moment of first contact affect collision outcomes?

My prediction: I think higher speeds will result in more severe collisions because the vehicle has more kinetic energy that has to go somewhere during the collision.

Observing Collisions - Data Collection

Video observations:

Collision Before collision After collision Notes
A Yellow cart moving right, blue cart stationary Yellow cart slowed down, blue cart started moving right Yellow transferred some of its speed to blue
B Yellow cart moving right faster, blue cart stationary Yellow cart nearly stopped, blue cart moving right faster than in A More initial speed = more speed transferred
C Yellow moving left, blue stationary Yellow changed direction (bounced), blue started moving left Direction reversed for yellow cart

Initial Explanations

M-E-F Triangle connections:

  • Motion: Carts change speeds during collision
  • Energy: Energy transfers from yellow cart to blue cart
  • Forces: Contact forces must be acting between the carts during collision

I think there must be contact forces between the two carts during collision. When they touch, they push on each other which changes their motion.

Predicting Force Interactions

Prediction: I predict that both carts experience equal forces but in opposite directions.

Evidence for my prediction:

  • Newton’s 3rd law - “for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction”
  • Both carts change motion, so both must experience forces
  • The carts are pushing against each other during contact

Understanding Force Data

Force graphs observations:

  • Forces only occur during brief contact between carts
  • Force on green cart is negative while force on blue cart is positive
  • The magnitude (size) of the forces appears to be the same
  • Forces last for the same amount of time

Interpreting Negative Force

Negative force means pushing to the LEFT Positive force means pushing to the RIGHT

The green cart experiences a negative force (pushed left) The blue cart experiences a positive force (pushed right)

BUT the magnitudes are the same! This confirms Newton’s 3rd law - equal and opposite forces.

Speed Data Analysis

Looking at the velocity-time graphs:

Collision A:

  • Yellow cart: Initial v ≈ 0.8 m/s, final v ≈ 0.3 m/s (slowed down)
  • Blue cart: Initial v = 0 m/s, final v ≈ 0.5 m/s (sped up)

Collision B:

  • Yellow cart: Initial v ≈ 1.5 m/s, final v ≈ 0.1 m/s (slowed down more)
  • Blue cart: Initial v = 0 m/s, final v ≈ 1.4 m/s (sped up more)

Collision C:

  • Yellow cart: Initial v ≈ -0.8 m/s, final v ≈ 0.3 m/s (changed direction)
  • Blue cart: Initial v = 0 m/s, final v ≈ -0.5 m/s (moved left)

PATTERN NOTICED: The amount of speed change seems to be the same for both carts!

Understanding Velocity vs. Speed

Velocity vs. Speed:

  • Speed = how fast something moves (magnitude only)
  • Velocity = speed WITH direction (vector quantity)

In our experiments:

  • RIGHT = positive velocity
  • LEFT = negative velocity

Example: -5 m/s means 5 meters per second to the LEFT

Notebook Activity: Velocity & Force

  1. How is velocity different from speed?
    • Velocity includes direction (vector), while speed is just magnitude (scalar)
    • Example: 60 mph north (velocity) vs. just 60 mph (speed)
  2. How have we expanded our understanding of force?
    • Forces are vectors with direction
    • Negative forces push left, positive forces push right
    • Equal and opposite forces occur in pairs (Newton’s 3rd Law)
    • Forces cause velocity changes
  3. Velocity-time graph:

  1. Distance calculation:

    First segment (triangle): d₁ = ½ × 4 m/s × 2s = 4m Second segment (rectangle): d₂ = 4 m/s × 3s = 12m Third segment (triangle): d₃ = ½ × 4 m/s × 2s = 4m

    Total distance = d₁ + d₂ + d₃ = 4m + 12m + 4m = 20m

Mass Effects on Collisions - Predictions

Collision D: Double both masses

  • Prediction: Same velocity changes (mass cancels out)
  • Force magnitude will probably be larger

Collision E: Double green cart (left) mass only

  • Prediction: Green cart will have less velocity change
  • Blue cart will have more velocity change

Collision F: Double blue cart (right) mass only

  • Prediction: Blue cart will have less velocity change
  • Green cart will have more velocity change

Mass Effects - Data Analysis

Observations from video:

Collision Mass ratio Velocity changes Notes
D 1:1 (both doubled) Similar to original Forces larger but Δv same
E 2:1 (green heavier) Green Δv smaller, Blue Δv larger Green harder to move
F 1:2 (blue heavier) Green Δv larger, Blue Δv smaller Blue harder to move

Key Finding: The cart with more mass has less velocity change!

Mathematical Relationships

Collision E Calculation (green cart 2× mass):

Green cart:

  • Initial v = 0.79 m/s
  • Final v = 0.33 m/s
  • Δv = 0.33 - 0.79 = -0.46 m/s

Blue cart:

  • Initial v = 0 m/s
  • Final v = 0.92 m/s
  • Δv = 0.92 - 0 = 0.92 m/s

Ratio of masses: m₁/m₂ = 2m/m = 2 Ratio of velocity changes: Δv₁/Δv₂ = -0.46/0.92 = -0.5

So: m₁/m₂ = -Δv₂/Δv₁ = 2

THE BIG FORMULA: m₁/m₂ = -Δv₂/Δv₁

This means: The ratio of masses equals the negative reciprocal of the ratio of velocity changes!

Checkpoint: Mass & Velocity Changes

  1. If a 3 kg cart collides with a 1 kg cart, ratio of velocity changes?

    m₁/m₂ = 3/1 = 3 m₁/m₂ = -Δv₂/Δv₁ 3 = -Δv₂/Δv₁ Δv₂/Δv₁ = -3

    The 1 kg cart’s velocity change will be 3 times larger than the 3 kg cart’s change.

  2. How would increasing mass affect velocity change?

    Increasing the mass of an object decreases its velocity change in a collision. If mass doubles, velocity change is halved.

  3. Why do smaller vehicles experience greater velocity changes?

    According to our formula m₁/m₂ = -Δv₂/Δv₁, the lighter vehicle (smaller m) will experience a proportionally larger velocity change (larger Δv). This is why collisions between trucks and cars are more dangerous for the car occupants.

  4. A 1500 kg car collides with a 3000 kg truck. Truck’s Δv = 2 m/s. Calculate car’s Δv.

    m₁/m₂ = -Δv₂/Δv₁ 1500/3000 = -Δv₁truck/Δvcar 1/2 = -2m/s/Δvcar Δvcar = -(2m/s ÷ 1/2) = -(2m/s × 2) = -4 m/s

    Car’s velocity change = 4 m/s (twice the truck’s change)

Real-World Applications

Problem: 20,000 kg truck collides with 20 kg shopping cart

  1. Mass ratio: m₁/m₂ = 20,000/20 = 1,000

  2. Expected velocity change ratio: m₁/m₂ = -Δv₂/Δv₁ 1,000 = -Δvcart/Δvtruck Δvcart/Δvtruck = -1,000

  3. If truck’s velocity changes by -0.01 m/s: Δvcart/(-0.01 m/s) = -1,000 Δvcart = -0.01 m/s × (-1,000) = 10 m/s

    Shopping cart’s velocity changes by 10 m/s (22 mph)!

    This is why momentum conservation is important for vehicle safety design.

Exit Ticket

  1. Define velocity and explain how it differs from speed:

    Velocity is a vector quantity that includes both speed (magnitude) and direction. Speed is just the magnitude portion without directional information. For example, 50 mph north is a velocity, while just 50 mph is a speed.

  2. Explain relationship between mass ratios and velocity change ratios:

    The ratio of masses equals the negative reciprocal of the ratio of velocity changes: m₁/m₂ = -Δv₂/Δv₁

    This means the more massive object experiences less velocity change, and the ratio is inversely proportional to the mass ratio.

  3. Why do heavier vehicles provide better protection in collisions?

    According to our mathematical relationship, a heavier vehicle experiences a smaller velocity change in a collision. Since injuries are related to rapid changes in velocity (acceleration/deceleration), occupants of heavier vehicles experience less violent motion changes, reducing injury risk. This is why SUVs are often considered “safer” than smaller cars in collisions.

  4. 1000 kg car collides with 2000 kg SUV. Car’s velocity changes by 6 m/s. Calculate SUV’s change.

    m₁/m₂ = -Δv₂/Δv₁ 1000/2000 = -ΔvSUV/Δvcar 1/2 = -ΔvSUV/6m/s ΔvSUV = -6m/s × (1/2) = -3 m/s

    The SUV’s velocity changes by 3 m/s, half the car’s change.
